name: Amazon Web Services

profile.campus: AWS Santa Clara facility, Silicon Valley, CA
profile.address: Agnew Road, Agnew, Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, 95054
profile.reading:
This building is mapped as an Amazon Web Services facility on Agnew Road in the Agnew area of Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, part of the long established Silicon Valley data center market. AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating that this research could confirm applies specifically to this mapped location, and no source found this session ties the Agnew Road tag to a named AWS project.

Two separately documented Amazon data center projects exist nearby in Santa Clara, and neither could be confirmed as a match to this exact coordinate. The better known one sits about three miles north at 2305 Mission College Boulevard. Filed by developer Oppidan Investment Company under City of Santa Clara file numbers PLN2019-14213 and CEQ2020-01077, that project proposes demolishing a 358,000 square foot office and research building and replacing it with two three story data center buildings totaling roughly 490,000 square feet, a 278,526 square foot first phase and a 211,425 square foot second phase, plus a new city owned electrical substation on the parcel's north side. Trade press coverage reports each building carrying 49.5 megavolt amperes of power capacity, with Silicon Valley Power building a new 60 kilovolt Freedom Circle Junction substation and roughly 9 megavolt amperes of interim service to support it, a roughly 26 month construction effort priced near 5.4 million dollars for the substation work alone, paid for by Oppidan on Amazon's behalf. Amazon is reported to have purchased that site in 2020 for about 100 million dollars. Separately, under California Energy Commission docket 19-SPPE-05, filed November 25, 2019 for a small power plant exemption, the same Mission College Boulevard project's backup power is described as 43 diesel fired emergency generators at 2.5 megawatts each plus two smaller house power units, a combined 78.1 megawatts of standby generation. The City of Santa Clara's own project listing marks this file archived, with a development review hearing dated August 2020 and no later public update confirming final approval or completion.

A second, unrelated Amazon transaction closed roughly three miles further south, where Amazon paid 237.8 million dollars for a 747,424 square foot former Owens Corning insulation factory site at 960 Central Expressway near San Jose Mineta International Airport, land a previous developer had proposed building out with warehouse or data center space before Amazon's purchase. That site's later use has not been confirmed as a data center in any source reviewed this session.

None of these three locations, the Mission College Boulevard project, the Central Expressway acquisition, or this Agnew Road point, has been confirmed by this research as the same building, and readers should treat the two better documented projects as regional context for Amazon's overall Santa Clara footprint rather than as facts about this specific mapped structure. Santa Clara's data center growth generally has taken the form of redevelopment of existing office, laboratory, or light industrial buildings rather than greenfield construction, reflecting the city's largely built out land supply, and Silicon Valley Power, the city's municipal electric utility, has separately stated that data centers already account for a majority of its total electricity sales.
profile.capacity_note: Not published for this specific mapped location. The City of Santa Clara's own project records disclose square footage for a separate, large data center project nearby (2305 Mission College Blvd, approximately 490,000 square feet across two buildings) that this research could not confirm corresponds to this exact registry entry.
profile.facility_note: AWS has not identified this specific building by name, construction date, or function in any source found for this page. Its correspondence to the City of Santa Clara's Mission College Blvd project record is not independently confirmed beyond general proximity and Amazon's separately reported acquisition of a former factory site in Santa Clara.
profile.research_note: Verified and rewritten 2026-09-06. Prior draft named the banned aggregators Baxtel and DataCenterMap directly in the public reading text and contained a semicolon, both house-style violations, now removed. Fresh research this session pulled the DCD article on Amazon's 960 Central Expressway acquisition, the DCD article on the Silicon Valley Power substation for the Mission College Blvd project, the CEC docket 19-SPPE-05 page, and the City of Santa Clara's own PLN2019-14213 project listing, all allowed source types. None of these establishes a confirmed match to this row's Agnew Road coordinate, so the reading presents both known nearby Amazon projects explicitly as unconfirmed regional context rather than asserting either is this building, consistent with the honesty requirement over completeness.
profile.regional_context: Santa Clara and the broader Silicon Valley corridor form one of the oldest commercial data center markets in the United States, hosting dozens of facilities from many colocation and cloud operators, including Digital Realty, Equinix, CoreSite, and Switch, in addition to Amazon and other hyperscalers. Silicon Valley Power, the City of Santa Clara's municipal electric utility, serves much of the city's data center load, and the city has separately weighed grid capacity constraints against new data center development in its own planning documents. Land in Santa Clara is largely built out, so new data center projects in the city frequently take the form of redevelopment of existing office, laboratory, or light industrial buildings, as in the Mission College Blvd project referenced above, rather than greenfield construction of the kind seen in Virginia, Ohio, or Oregon.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Indiana campus, New Carlisle, St. Joseph County
profile.address: Western Avenue, Saint Joseph County, Indiana, 46552
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates near New Carlisle in St. Joseph County, Indiana, part of AWS's Northern Indiana data center campus near South Bend. AWS and Indiana state officials announced the original investment in this campus, put at $11 billion, in 2024; the Indianapolis Business Journal, DataCenterDynamics, and Inside INdiana Business all covered the announcement, and Amazon later broke ground on the campus per Northwest Indiana Business Magazine's coverage of the groundbreaking. On November 24, 2025, Amazon announced on its own aboutamazon.com news page a further $15 billion investment in Northern Indiana data center campuses, on top of the earlier commitment, framed as adding up to 2.4 gigawatts of data center capacity to the region, with a further gigawatt of grid capacity beyond Amazon's own needs also planned. Amazon's release put the new investment at generating roughly 1,100 new high-skilled direct jobs plus thousands of additional supply-chain jobs in construction, electrical work, and fiber-optic technician roles, and said the added grid capacity was projected to save existing Indiana households and businesses about $1 billion in electricity costs over 15 years. Amazon's release also disclosed that its cumulative investment in Indiana across all business lines, including its data centers, fulfillment network, and delivery stations, had exceeded $31.3 billion since 2010, supporting an estimated 24,500 direct and 27,500 indirect jobs and contributing more than $29.9 billion to the state's economy.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or an IT power rating specific to this individual building distinct from the regional gigawatt figures disclosed for the Northern Indiana campus as a whole, and no source found for this page breaks that campus down building by building.

profile.campus: AWS Mississippi -- Madison County campus (Ridgeland/Canton industrial parks)
profile.address: Highland Colony Parkway, New Hope Grove, Ridgeland, Madison County, Mississippi, 39157
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services is developing in Madison County, Mississippi, across two industrial park sites near Ridgeland and Canton, north of Jackson. The Mississippi Development Authority announced the project on January 25, 2024, describing it as a $10 billion private sector investment, the single largest capital investment in Mississippi history and about four times the size of the state's previous largest economic development project, expected to create at least 1,000 high-paying technology jobs. Governor Tate Reeves and the Development Authority did not name the investor at the time of the initial announcement; DataCenterDynamics and other trade press subsequently confirmed Amazon Web Services as the company behind the project.

Local Madison County press, including the Northside Sun and Canton-area coverage, and construction industry publications reported that multiple regional contractors were engaged to build what was described as twin AWS data centers on the two industrial park sites. Later state and company references cited investment figures beyond the original $10 billion as the project moved through additional phases; those later, larger figures were not independently confirmed against an AWS-owned or state-owned source for this page and should be read as a sequence of expanding announcements rather than one settled total.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no source found for this page breaks the Madison County campus down building by building. This structure is treated as part of the documented AWS Mississippi footprint described above. Mississippi state officials, including Governor Reeves, framed the project publicly as a turning point intended to diversify the state economy beyond its traditional manufacturing and agriculture base, and Madison County has since seen a series of related road, water, and utility infrastructure discussions at the county and state level tied directly to the AWS buildout.

Verified via fresh web search/fetch this session (not reused from 2026-09-02 batch without re-checking): AWS aboutamazon.com investment pages, state/city economic development releases, and named trade/local press, listed in sources. Prior batch's disclosure_policy claim (citing aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/ as directly confirming a non-disclosure policy) was checked directly this session and found to be overstated -- that page does not discuss facility-level disclosure at all -- so it was not reused verbatim; the non-disclosure finding here rests instead on the absence of building-level figures across every source checked, consistent with trade-press characterization of AWS's practice.
profile.regional_context: Madison County, Mississippi had no established hyperscale data center presence before AWS's January 2024 announcement, making the project a first-of-its-kind for the state rather than an addition to an existing cluster of the kind found in Virginia, Ohio, or Oregon. The Mississippi Development Authority's incentive package for the project was structured through the state's economic development statutes covering large scale private investment and required legislative action to finalize incentive terms, according to Mississippi Development Authority and state coverage. The project's scale relative to the state's prior economic development history, and its water and power demands in a market without existing large data center infrastructure, have been recurring subjects of Mississippi press coverage since the announcement.

profile.campus: AWS Ohio (US-EAST-2) -- New Albany campus, Franklin / Licking / Union counties
profile.address: Darree Fields Southeast, Dublin, Washington Township, Franklin County, Ohio, 43002
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates around New Albany, Ohio, a Columbus suburb spanning Franklin, Licking, and Union counties, the physical location of AWS's US-EAST-2 cloud region.

AWS's Ohio buildout has been documented in stages by the company, the City of New Albany, and Ohio trade and local press. The City of New Albany reported in August 2025 that AWS's cumulative capital investment in the area had reached $6.2 billion since 2015, that AWS had invested $19.7 billion across Ohio over that period, and that AWS operations in New Albany had contributed $1.4 billion to Licking County gross domestic product; the city's release also cited a further $10 billion in Ohio expansion AWS announced in 2024 and a forecast $23 billion cumulative investment by 2030. In August 2023, New Albany City Council approved a further $3.5 billion AWS investment covering five additional data center buildings, according to 10TV and Data Center Frontier coverage of that council vote. CoStar separately reported in 2024 that AWS's disclosed Ohio data center investment had grown by a further $10 billion. The City of New Albany's 2025 release stated AWS had completed and staffed two data center buildings in the area, with additional facilities under construction and expected to become operational later that year, and that AWS-related activity supported an estimated 1,550 full time equivalent jobs annually in Licking County and paid $3.1 million in property taxes and fees to the county in 2024.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and none of the city, county, or trade press coverage found for this page breaks the New Albany campus down building by building. This structure is treated as part of the documented AWS Ohio footprint described above.

profile.regional_context: New Albany, a Columbus, Ohio suburb, has become one of the Midwest's fastest growing data center markets since AWS selected the area for its Ohio cloud region in the mid-2010s. American Electric Power's Ohio utility serves the corridor and has filed with state regulators over large-load data center interconnection requests as the New Albany, Licking County, and Union County buildout has expanded. Ohio offers a data center sales and use tax exemption administered by the state Development Services Agency, tied to minimum investment and payroll commitments, which local officials and trade press credit with drawing AWS and other operators to the corridor. New Albany markets itself alongside Intel's nearby semiconductor investment in Licking County as part of a broader technology corridor sometimes called the Silicon Heartland, and hosts data center campuses for other operators including Meta and Google in addition to AWS. Local governments in New Albany, Licking County, and Union County have negotiated a series of tax abatement and community benefit agreements with AWS, documented in city council minutes and covered by 10TV and Data Center Frontier.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and none of the city, county, or trade press coverage found for this page breaks the New Albany campus down building by building. AWS does not publish a per-building street address, opening date, square footage, or IT power rating for this structure; none of the sources checked break the named campus down building by building. Prior batch's disclosure_policy claim (citing aws.amazon.com/about-aws/global-infrastructure/regions_az/ as directly confirming a non-disclosure policy) was checked directly this session and found to be overstated -- that page does not discuss facility-level disclosure at all -- so it was not reused verbatim; the non-disclosure finding here rests instead on the absence of building-level figures across every source checked, consistent with trade-press characterization of AWS's practice.
profile.regional_context: New Albany, a Columbus, Ohio suburb, has become one of the Midwest's fastest growing data center markets since AWS selected the area for its Ohio cloud region in the mid-2010s. American Electric Power's Ohio utility serves the corridor and has filed with state regulators over large-load data center interconnection requests as the New Albany, Licking County, and Union County buildout has expanded. Ohio offers a data center sales and use tax exemption administered by the state Development Services Agency, tied to minimum investment and payroll commitments, which local officials and trade press credit with drawing AWS and other operators to the corridor. New Albany markets itself alongside Intel's nearby semiconductor investment in Licking County as part of a broader technology corridor sometimes called the Silicon Heartland, and hosts data center campuses for other operators including Meta and Google in addition to AWS. Local governments in New Albany, Licking County, and Union County have negotiated a series of tax abatement and community benefit agreements with AWS, documented in city council minutes and covered by 10TV and Data Center Frontier.

profile.campus: AWS Ohio (US-EAST-2) -- New Albany campus, Franklin / Licking / Union counties
profile.address: Newton Court, Amazon New Albany: Innovation Campus Way, New Albany, Jersey Township, Licking County, Ohio
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates around New Albany, Ohio, a Columbus suburb spanning Franklin, Licking, and Union counties, the physical location of AWS's US-EAST-2 cloud region.

AWS's Ohio buildout has been documented in stages by the company, the City of New Albany, and Ohio trade and local press. The City of New Albany reported in August 2025 that AWS's cumulative capital investment in the area had reached $6.2 billion since 2015, that AWS had invested $19.7 billion across Ohio over that period, and that AWS operations in New Albany had contributed $1.4 billion to Licking County gross domestic product; the city's release also cited a further $10 billion in Ohio expansion AWS announced in 2024 and a forecast $23 billion cumulative investment by 2030. In August 2023, New Albany City Council approved a further $3.5 billion AWS investment covering five additional data center buildings, according to 10TV and Data Center Frontier coverage of that council vote. CoStar separately reported in 2024 that AWS's disclosed Ohio data center investment had grown by a further $10 billion. The City of New Albany's 2025 release stated AWS had completed and staffed two data center buildings in the area, with additional facilities under construction and expected to become operational later that year, and that AWS-related activity supported an estimated 1,550 full time equivalent jobs annually in Licking County and paid $3.1 million in property taxes and fees to the county in 2024.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and none of the city, county, or trade press coverage found for this page breaks the New Albany campus down building by building. This structure is treated as part of the documented AWS Ohio footprint described above.

profile.community_note: Hilliard asked AEP and Bloom Energy to add carbon capture, citing CO2 volume and resident health. Modelling commissioned by the city and published February 2026 found the plant would raise CO2 by about 27.7 ppm at the nearest home 800 feet away and about 3.6 ppm at Beacon Elementary School 4,000 feet away, against an ambient 350 to 450 ppm and a health threshold generally taken to begin near 5,000 ppm. A second independent study in May 2026 confirmed the method. Ohio EPA did not set a CO2 limit in the air permit because other regulated pollutants fall below federal thresholds.
profile.incentives_note: A Community Reinvestment Act agreement with Hilliard abates property tax on data centre buildings against a $200 million investment by 31 December 2026, which the city states Amazon has met or exceeded. Hilliard City School District receives up to $3.4 million a year: $400,000 plus $1.50 per square foot of building, against up to two million square feet planned.
profile.regulatory_note: The plant is exempt from Hilliard zoning: Ohio Revised Code 4906.13(B) gives the Ohio Power Siting Board exclusive jurisdiction over generation above 50 MW, and no local government may permit or condition a facility holding an OPSB certificate.

profile.campus: Marysville Innovation Park, 55 acres, two buildings
profile.address: 14684 Industrial Parkway, Marysville, Union County, OH 43040
profile.reading:
Amazon Web Services Marysville, known during planning as Project Cosmo, is a two-building data centre campus on 55 acres at 14684 Industrial Parkway in the Marysville Innovation Park, Union County, Ohio. AWS filed a rezoning application in October 2024, applied for the project in February 2025, and received a reinvestment area agreement from Marysville City Council on 10 March 2025. The company committed to investing $1 billion, with the two buildings totalling 500,000 square feet. Construction was slated to begin in August 2025 and to complete in 2027.

No IT capacity figure has been published for the campus, and the two numbers that are published should not be mistaken for one. The $1 billion is committed investment and the 500,000 square feet is floor area; neither indicates how much compute the site will carry. AWS does not publish per-facility power for its own buildings, and Union County has not required it to.

What Marysville did publish is the price. The reinvestment area agreement carries a thirty-year, 100 percent exemption from property tax on the assessed value of the data centres. Against that, AWS committed to $15 million a year for fifteen years to the Marysville Exempted Village School District and the city, plus other community support. A thirty-year full abatement against a fifteen-year payment is the shape of most data-centre agreements in the state, and the arithmetic of that trade is a matter of public record rather than of estimate.

The campus sits within a much larger central Ohio build-out. AWS has said it spent more than $10 billion on infrastructure in Ohio in the decade to 2025, and in 2023 stated plans for roughly $7.8 billion more by the end of the decade, of which about $3.5 billion was directed at a five-building campus in New Albany. Since then the company has announced a $2 billion campus at Sunbury and acquired 590 acres in Jefferson Township, Fayette County. Marysville is one site in that programme, not a standalone project, and its power will be drawn from the same constrained central Ohio grid that led AEP and Amazon to install 72.9 MW of fuel cells at the Scioto Darby campus in Hilliard, about twenty miles south.

This entry is built from the city council decision as reported and from AWS statements. It is not yet mapped in OpenStreetMap, which is why it carries a press identifier rather than a way identifier: the buildings were still under construction when this registry last harvested the map.

profile.campus: AWS Oregon (US-WEST-2) -- Boardman / Umatilla / Hermiston campus, Morrow & Umatilla counties
profile.address: 988, East Penney Avenue, Hermiston, Umatilla County, Oregon, 97838
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Morrow and Umatilla counties in eastern Oregon, near the towns of Boardman, Umatilla, and Hermiston along the Columbia River. This is among AWS's original hyperscale campus locations, chosen for proximity to relatively low cost hydroelectric power generated along the Columbia River system, and it has expanded substantially since AWS's first Oregon buildings went up in the early 2010s.

Amazon's own aboutamazon.com materials on the region's economic impact state that AWS invested $15.6 billion in Morrow and Umatilla counties between 2012 and 2021, contributing $1.1 billion to local gross domestic product, and that AWS supported more than 1,800 full time direct employees across the two counties along with thousands of additional local jobs in construction, facilities maintenance, and electricity generation. Amazon states its Oregon data centers pay the highest local tax contributions in both counties, that it recycles roughly 96 percent of its cooling water back to local farmers at no charge, and that it draws at least 95 percent of the electricity powering the campus from renewable sources. Oregon Public Broadcasting and DataCenterDynamics have reported on AWS's continued expansion in Hermiston and Morrow County since 2025, including additional land acquisitions and plans local coverage ties to AI-focused, large scale data center construction, alongside continuing state and local tax abatements under Oregon's strategic investment program.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no source found for this page breaks the Morrow/Umatilla County AWS campus down building by building. This structure is treated as part of the documented AWS Oregon footprint described above.

Water rights and cooling water use have become a recurring local policy issue as the campus has expanded, covered by Oregon Public Broadcasting and regional outlets. The Boardman-Hermiston corridor is also drawing interest from other data center developers citing the same power and land availability that first attracted AWS, per Data Center Frontier reporting on competing projects in the area.

profile.campus: AWS Oregon (US-WEST-2) -- Boardman / Umatilla / Hermiston campus, Morrow & Umatilla counties
profile.address: 75288, Lewis and Clark Drive, Boardman, Morrow County, Oregon, 97818
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Morrow and Umatilla counties in eastern Oregon, near the towns of Boardman, Umatilla, and Hermiston along the Columbia River. This is among AWS's original hyperscale campus locations, chosen for proximity to relatively low cost hydroelectric power generated along the Columbia River system, and it has expanded substantially since AWS's first Oregon buildings went up in the early 2010s.

Amazon's own aboutamazon.com materials on the region's economic impact state that AWS invested $15.6 billion in Morrow and Umatilla counties between 2012 and 2021, contributing $1.1 billion to local gross domestic product, and that AWS supported more than 1,800 full time direct employees across the two counties along with thousands of additional local jobs in construction, facilities maintenance, and electricity generation. Amazon states its Oregon data centers pay the highest local tax contributions in both counties, that it recycles roughly 96 percent of its cooling water back to local farmers at no charge, and that it draws at least 95 percent of the electricity powering the campus from renewable sources. Oregon Public Broadcasting and DataCenterDynamics have reported on AWS's continued expansion in Hermiston and Morrow County since 2025, including additional land acquisitions and plans local coverage ties to AI-focused, large scale data center construction, alongside continuing state and local tax abatements under Oregon's strategic investment program.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no source found for this page breaks the Morrow/Umatilla County AWS campus down building by building. This structure is treated as part of the documented AWS Oregon footprint described above.

profile.campus: AWS / Talen Energy Susquehanna nuclear-adjacent campus, Berwick, Columbia County, PA
profile.address: Amazon AWS PHL, 1125, Electron Avenue, Berwick, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, 18603
profile.reading:
This building sits on Electron Avenue at 1125, a mailing address of Berwick, Pennsylvania, though the parcel itself lies across the Susquehanna River on the grounds of the Susquehanna Steam Electric Station, a two unit nuclear plant in Salem Township, Luzerne County. The 300,000 square foot structure was built by Cumulus Data, a subsidiary Talen Energy created specifically to develop data center space on land it owned around the nuclear plant. Cumulus broke ground in December 2021 and announced the powered shell as complete in January 2023, describing it as the first of a planned campus of roughly six buildings meant to draw directly on the plant's low carbon output. Talen sold the entire 1,200 acre campus, including this first completed building, to Amazon Web Services in March 2024 for 650 million dollars, in what CoStar identified as the largest single commercial real estate sale in the United States that year.

What followed was a genuinely unusual regulatory fight, and it is worth recounting because it is the actual local and national record for this site. Talen and PJM Interconnection asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve an amended interconnection agreement that would have let Amazon draw power directly from the plant behind the meter, first at 300 megawatts, then expanded in 120 megawatt increments toward a ceiling of 960 megawatts. Exelon and American Electric Power intervened against the arrangement, arguing it shifted grid costs onto other ratepayers, and on November 1, 2024, FERC rejected the amended agreement on a 2 to 1 vote, with Chairman Willie Phillips dissenting on reliability grounds. Talen and Amazon did not walk away. In June 2025 the two companies restructured the deal entirely, moving from a behind the meter co location model to what Talen called a front of the meter arrangement, Susquehanna sells its output into the PJM grid as it always has, Talen becomes a retail electric supplier to Amazon under a power purchase agreement running through 2042, and PPL Electric Utilities carries the power over its transmission system rather than a private wire. The companies expect the transmission reconfiguration to take effect in spring 2026, timed to a planned refueling outage at the plant, with volume ramping toward a stated 1,920 megawatts of nuclear output by 2032.

None of those campus scale figures describe this single building. The 1125 Electron Avenue structure itself was reported by DatacenterDynamics at 48 megawatts of capacity, a number tied to the original Cumulus Data shell rather than to any Amazon operated IT load, and no source found in this research states a critical IT load, a diesel standby figure, or an onsite generation figure specific to this building under Amazon's operation. Given the scale of construction reported in trade press since the 2024 sale, it is likely additional buildings have gone up on the same parcel since, but this record concerns the single mapped structure. What remains undocumented publicly is the current occupancy status of the original Cumulus shell, any Luzerne County permit numbers tied to its later fitout by Amazon, and any tax agreement specific to this parcel, as opposed to the statewide sales tax exemption on data center equipment that Pennsylvania has offered under a 2016 law expanded in 2021.

Neither company has broken these figures down to this specific building.

profile.community_note: Pennsylvania's Department of Community and Economic Development framed Amazon's wider Pennsylvania investment, which spans this Luzerne County campus and a second site in Bucks County, as worth at least 1,250 permanent high tech jobs, alongside thousands of construction positions and a 10 million dollar state commitment to local workforce training. Reporting since has cautioned that permanent onsite roles at data centers of this kind tend toward security, landscaping, and a small technical staff rather than large payrolls, and neither Salem Township nor Berwick borough has published its own count of jobs or tax revenue tied specifically to this building.
profile.regional_context: The Susquehanna nuclear plant, operated by Talen Energy near Berwick in Columbia County, Pennsylvania, sits within the PJM Interconnection, the regional grid operator covering most of Pennsylvania and a swath of the mid-Atlantic and Midwest. AWS's arrangement there is among the highest-profile examples nationally of a hyperscale cloud operator contracting directly for nuclear power to serve a data center campus, and it drew regulatory scrutiny from FERC and objections from grid operators including AEP Ohio and Exelon before the companies restructured the deal as a standard grid power purchase agreement. Pennsylvania's broader push to attract data center investment, including Amazon's $20 billion statewide commitment, has been publicly framed by Governor Josh Shapiro's administration as a strategy to pair the state's existing nuclear and gas generation capacity with new large-load industrial demand.

profile.campus: AWS San Antonio-area facilities, Bexar County, TX
profile.address: Micron Drive, San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas, 78245
profile.reading:
Mapping data identifies this building as an Amazon Web Services facility near Micron Drive in San Antonio, Bexar County, Texas. This research could not locate a well known "Micron Drive" in the far west Bexar County data center corridor that trade press and local reporting usually describe, and could not rule out that the street name in the underlying map data is an approximation or a variant spelling of a nearby road. The stored coordinates place the building closer to central San Antonio, inside Loop 1604 on the city's west side, rather than in the far western Potranco Road, Omicron Drive, and Highway 151 corridor where the San Antonio Report says more than 30 data centers have already been built and at least 23 more are planned as of 2026, with CyrusOne and Vantage Data Centers alone registering more than $1 billion in construction there since 2020. That corridor is also home to Vantage projects the same reporting describes as carrying 423 megawatts of dedicated onsite generation supplied by VoltaGrid natural gas plants, a level of onsite generation specific to Vantage's own sites and not something this research found any basis to attribute to this Amazon building.

Trade press has reported two distinct 2026 Amazon Data Services filings in the San Antonio area through Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation records, a project at 12807 Donop Road valued near 65 million dollars and roughly 120,000 square feet with construction expected to begin in March 2026 and finish in February 2029, and a separate COPT-applicant project at 1535 NW Crossroads valued near 25 million dollars and about 141,979 square feet, that filing naming an AWS engineer as tenant contact, with construction beginning around October 2026. Neither filing's address matches the Micron Drive location stored for this row closely enough for this research to confirm either one as this specific building. Amazon is widely reported to acquire United States data center real estate through a subsidiary named Vadata, Inc. rather than directly under the Amazon.com or AWS names, the same practice reported at AWS campuses in Virginia, Ohio, and Oregon, but this research did not pull a Bexar County Appraisal District parcel record for this exact coordinate to confirm Vadata or another Amazon-linked entity as the owner here. San Antonio and Bexar County have become one of Texas's most active data center markets, with the Data Center Coalition industry group counting Amazon, Microsoft, and Google among its members active in the region, and CPS Energy, the city owned electric utility, supplying power locally under negotiated large load agreements rather than the Public Utility Commission of Texas process that governs most investor owned utilities elsewhere in the state.
profile.capacity_note: Not published at the individual building level for this specific coordinate. Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation permit filings reported in local and trade press disclose square footage and cost estimates for three separate San Antonio-area Amazon data center projects filed in March 2026, but this research could not confirm which filing, if any, corresponds to this exact registry entry.
profile.facility_note: AWS has not identified this specific building by name, construction date, or function in any source found for this page. Multiple Amazon data center projects have been reported in the San Antonio area; this entry's correspondence to any one of them is not independently confirmed beyond its mapped coordinates and street reference.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: 4101, Westfax Drive, Chantilly, Fairfax County, Virginia, 20153
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: 21320, Beaumeade Circle, Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia, 20147
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: Statesboro Place, Brambleton, Loudoun County, Virginia, 20105
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: 22945, International Drive, Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia, 20166
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: 44858, Interconnection Plaza, Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia, 20147
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.campus: AWS Northern Virginia (Data Center Alley) -- US-EAST-1 region, Loudoun / Prince William / Fairfax counties
profile.address: Prince William Parkway, Innovation, Prince William County, Virginia, 20156
profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.reading:
This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

This building is one of the data center structures Amazon Web Services operates in Northern Virginia, within the corridor of eastern Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties that the data center industry calls Data Center Alley, described in trade press as the largest concentration of data centers in the world. AWS traces its Virginia data center presence back to 2006, making this one of the company's original hyperscale cloud regions, now designated US-EAST-1. The corridor grew up around the MAE-East internet exchange point that formed near Tysons and Ashburn in the 1990s, which drew network carriers and later cloud and colocation operators to locate near dense fiber connectivity.

AWS's own public affairs materials, published on aboutamazon.com, state that the company invested $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenses on its Virginia data center infrastructure between 2011 and 2021, and in January 2023 announced a further $35 billion committed to build additional data center campuses across Virginia through 2040. AWS reports its Virginia operations generated $8.2 billion in regional GDP over 2011 to 2021, supported an average of 7,340 full time equivalent jobs at local businesses across that period, and employed 8,710 people directly in the state by 2021, a figure AWS later put at more than 8,800. In 2022, AWS paid $334 million in Virginia business personal property tax. AWS also states it operates 18 solar farms in Virginia generating roughly 2.9 million megawatt hours of clean energy annually, enough by its own estimate to power about 276,000 homes, and that approximately 70 percent of global internet traffic moves through data centers located in the state.

AWS has not published a street address, opening date, floor area, or IT power rating for this individual building, and no county or state economic development record found for this page breaks the Virginia AWS footprint down building by building. What is documented is that this structure sits within the AWS data center footprint the company has confirmed for the Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax county corridor, described by the investment, employment, and tax figures above, which report the regional AWS buildout rather than this specific structure.

profile.regional_context: Northern Virginia is described in trade press as the largest data center market in the world by capacity, anchored by the Loudoun County corridor known as Data Center Alley and now extending into Prince William, Fairfax, and neighboring counties. Alongside AWS, the corridor hosts large campuses operated by Digital Realty, Equinix, Microsoft, Google, Meta, QTS, and CloudHQ, among others. Power for the region comes primarily from Dominion Energy, which has repeatedly identified data center demand as the fastest growing category on its system and has sought new transmission and generation capacity to keep pace. Virginia exempts qualifying data center equipment purchases from state and local sales and use tax under a program administered by the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, an incentive credited by local officials with accelerating the buildout. Local zoning disputes over new campuses, water use for cooling, and Dominion grid capacity have been a recurring subject in Loudoun and Prince William county government since the early 2020s, reported by Virginia Business, Data Center Frontier, and Inside Climate News.

profile.global_infrastructure: 124 Availability Zones within 39 Geographic Regions as of source date; 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more Regions (Saudi Arabia, Chile) announced but not yet live

reading:
Amazon Web Services began as an internal Amazon project in July 2002, launched Simple Queue Service in 2004, then reached its modern form with S3 in March 2006 and EC2 in August 2006. It operates as a business segment of Amazon.com, Inc., a public company trading as AMZN, SEC filer CIK 0001018724, headquartered at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington.

As of the source date, AWS states its cloud spans 124 Availability Zones across 39 geographic regions worldwide, with 7 more Availability Zones and 2 more regions, in Saudi Arabia and Chile, announced but not yet live. Within the United States, AWS names Northern Virginia, Ohio, Northern California, and Oregon as public regions, plus two GovCloud regions serving government workloads. The registry here tracks 243 AWS facilities across seven states, California, Mississippi, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Texas, and Virginia, with the largest concentration in Northern Virginia's Loudoun, Prince William, and Fairfax counties, the corridor widely known as Data Center Alley.

Amazon has disclosed specific investment figures for Virginia: $51.9 billion in capital and operating expenditure from 2011 through 2021, an additional $35 billion planned for data center campuses through 2040, and $8.2 billion in GDP contribution over the 2011 to 2021 period. The company reported paying $334 million in business personal property taxes in 2022 and employing 8,710 people supporting Virginia data center operations in 2021. Amazon also states it has built or contracted 18 solar farms in Virginia, stated to generate enough power to serve about 276,000 homes.

These figures describe AWS's own reported investment and power posture in its largest US buildout state, not facility by facility specifications. Virginia's position as AWS's most concentrated US buildout, backed by declared multi decade capital commitments and utility scale solar contracting, is a direct instance of the compute, power, and buildings link this site tracks: cloud capacity growth here is paired with explicit, dollar denominated grid and land investment rather than compute alone.
